extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Latin literature; poets/readers interested in Horatian conduct and poetic craft
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles drawn from Horace's Epistles on (a) the social conduct of a protegé toward a patron and (b) poetic practice (imitation, originality, publication, and performance). Useful for composing Horatian epistles or imitating his poetics and social advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid being a parasite; avoid offensive independence
rubrics_metrics.description: A true friend, Lollius, never plays the parasite, yet on the other hand never shows his independence by rudeness or by insistence upon trifles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strike a mean between obsequious flattery and blunt rudeness; comport yourself with decorum rather than servility or boorish bluntness (Epistle XVIII, opening lines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not emulate patron's ostentation or weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: As protege, you must not try to emulate your patron in his ostentation or other weaknesses, for you will merely earn his contempt or hatred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid copying the patron's visible vices/vanities; imitation of such traits leads to loss of respect rather than favour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep entrusted secrets faithfully
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither should you pry into his secrets, though if he entrust any to you you must keep them faithfully (even under wine or anger).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not investigate a patron's private affairs; if confided in, resist all inducements (wine, anger) to betray confidences — confidentiality is a core duty of the protegé.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt to patron's tastes and moods; be agreeable
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not emphasize your own tastes in contrast with your patron's. If he wishes to go a‑hunting, put your books aside... He must fall in with his patron's moods and at all times show a cheery face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Yielding personal preferences to share the patron's pastimes (hunting, festivals) demonstrates tact and secures goodwill; maintain a cheerful demeanour rather than moralizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise discretion in criticism and introductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Be discreet in your criticism of others; covet not your patron's slaves; be careful to introduce only people who will not humiliate you later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vet those you recommend or introduce; public association carries risk—choose people whose faults won't reflect on you, and avoid envy-driven or tactless remarks about others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge mistakes to preserve later credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Should you make a mistake, don't fail to acknowledge it, so that, if necessary, you may be able to defend those who really deserve your aid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admitting error preserves trust and positions you to shield worthy allies in future controversies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid tattlers and gossipers; guard what you say and to whom
rubrics_metrics.description: Think often of what you say, and of whom, and to whom you say it. Avoid a questioner, for he is also a tattler... and the word once let slip flies beyond recall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from confiding in inquisitive or garrulous people; never assume a spoken word can be recalled — discretion in speech protects you and your patron.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid romantic entanglements in patron's household
rubrics_metrics.description: Let no maid or boy within your worshipful friend's marble threshold inflame your heart, lest the owner of the pretty boy or dear girl make you happy with a present so trifling or torment you if disobliging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from illicit attachments to servants/young people in a patron's household to avoid awkward obligations, punishments, or loss of favour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate moderation and tranquility through learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Above all, you must study the words of the wise and learn the secret of a tranquil life... read and question the wise, how you may be able to pass your days in tranquillity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursue philosophical study to determine what lessens cares and produces a balanced mind (virtue, honour, modest possessions, seclusion, books); rely on reasoned choice as much as on prayer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation of lifestyle — avoid intemperance (wine)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you follow old Cratinus... no poems can please long, nor live, which are written by water‑drinkers. Homer is convicted as a winebibber; Ennius never sprang forth to tell of arms save after much drinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace warns against the excesses of drink and the reputation of poets as intemperate; self‑control and sobriety are implied conditions of lasting poetic reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject slavish imitation; imitate spirit, not mere words
rubrics_metrics.description: O imitatores, servum pecus... I was the first to show to Latium the iambics of Paros, following the rhythms and spirit of Archilochus, not the themes or the words that hounded Lycambes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use classical models freely but avoid servile copying; borrow meters, rhythms, or manner while producing original subject‑matter and voice; be an innovator within tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not write to defame or to injure others with verse
rubrics_metrics.description: Sappho/Alcaeus temper the Muse... nor seeks a father‑in‑law whom he besmears with black verses, nor weaves a noose for his bride with scandalous rhyme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using poetry as a weapon to defame, blacken reputations, or entangle private lives — ethical restraint in content is part of artistic integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not pander for popular or aristocratic votes (no bribery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non ego ventosae plebis suffragia venor... non ego, nobilium scriptorum auditor et ultor — I do not court the votes of a fickle public at the cost of suppers and gifts of worn‑out clothes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist seeking applause or patronage by bribery, flattery, or pandering to learned teachers and 'noble' circles; write for artistic reasons rather than transactional gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gladiatorial public recitations that breed strife
rubrics_metrics.description: Spissis indigna theatris scripta pudet recitare... 'The place you choose suits me not,' I cry, and call for a truce in the sports. Ludus enim genuit trepidum certamen et iram; ira truces inimicitias et funebre bellum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public contests of wit (recitals in crowded theatres) encourage rivalry, anger, and destructive quarrels; choose contexts of presentation that avoid fomenting hostile contests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared for the public life and eventual fate of your book
rubrics_metrics.description: You seem, my book... when you are once let out, there will be no coming back... when you've been well thumbed by vulgar hands and begin to grow soiled, you will either be food for moths, or run away to Utica, or be sent to be a schoolbook for lads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that publication exposes a work to praise, neglect, mutilation, misuse, or pedagogical reduction; accept the inevitability of various receptions and losses of control once a work enters public circulation.
